claims.text: Advanced multi-principal-element high-entropy alloys can be lightweight while providing superior comprehensive performance.
The material begins in an as-cast state.
The as-cast material has a disordered crystal structure.
The alloy contains a combination of principal elements such as Fe, Co, Ni, Cr, and Mn.
Composition adjustment can produce a high-entropy state.
The proposed composition forms a single-phase FCC solid solution.
The FCC solid solution has a high degree of lattice distortion.
The high-entropy alloy exhibits sluggish diffusion kinetics.
Increased lattice distortion makes dislocation movement more difficult and thereby enhances strength.
Sluggish diffusion reduces the rate of corrosion reactions and thereby enhances corrosion resistance.
The high-entropy alloy will have at least 20% greater yield strength than 316L stainless steel under the same operating conditions.
The high-entropy alloy will have at least 30% lower density than 316L stainless steel.
316L stainless steel has a yield strength of 290 MPa.
316L stainless steel has a density of 7.9 g/cm^3.
Each principal element should be present at 0.5–2.0 atomic percent.
Departing from the stated 0.5–2.0 atomic-percent range may reduce performance or stability.

contradictions.description: The material is described as a multi-principal-element/high-entropy alloy, but the requirement that each of the five named principal elements constitute only 0.5–2.0 at.% accounts for just 2.5–10 at.% in total and does not specify the remaining 90–97.5 at.%; this is internally inconsistent with treating those named elements as the principal composition.
